requirements: The core contributions of the paper 'Improving Efficiency of GPU Kernel Optimization Agents using a Domain-Specific Language and Speed-of-Light Guidance' have been reproduced: the µCUTLASS DSL/compiler, SOL analysis, MANTIS SOL-guided steering (in-prompt and orchestrated), SOL-guided budget scheduling, and SOL-guided integrity checking, evaluated across GPT-5-mini/GPT-5/GPT-5.2 on the 59-problem KernelBench subset.

sub_tasks.requirements: H100 (SM90a) node with locked GPU clocks, NGC container (PyTorch 2.10.0a0 / CUDA 13.0), Nsight Compute (NCU) profiling, CUTLASS 3.x installed, cutlass_cppgen extended for EVT emission, and OpenHands agent runtime are available and configured.
The physical GPU node exposes an H100 (SM90a) with clocks locked to a deterministic fixed frequency so kernel timings do not drift with DVFS.
Code has been implemented that queries the GPU device and verifies the reported architecture is SM90a (Hopper H100); the run aborts or logs a hard error if a non-SM90a device is detected.

Code has been implemented that locks the H100 clocks to a fixed frequency (e.g., via nvidia-smi -lgc / --lock-gpu-clocks) before any timing measurement is taken, and unlocks or restores them on teardown.

Code has been implemented that records the actual clock frequency queried from nvidia-smi at run time into the run manifest, so that SOL analysis and reproduction reports can use the true clocks (falling back to a 1500 MHz default only when the query fails).
The software container matches the paper's NGC-based stack: PyTorch 2.10.0a0 with CUDA 13.0, containerized via Docker for parity across cluster nodes.
Code / Dockerfile has been implemented that builds from an NGC image providing PyTorch 2.10.0a0, and a runtime assertion verifies torch.__version__.startswith('2.10.0a0').
The CUDA toolkit inside the container is version 13.0 (nvcc --version reports 13.0); the build system uses this nvcc to compile driver.cpp / cuda_model.cu.

A Docker container definition (Dockerfile or compose spec) is provided and the pipeline launches every per-problem workspace inside that container, giving byte-identical toolchains across cluster nodes.
Nsight Compute (NCU) is installed and used as the sole timer for on-GPU kernel execution time, excluding launch overhead, host-device sync, and Python framework latency.
Code has been implemented that locates the ncu binary in the container and exposes a compile/run/profile Makefile target invoking it with appropriate metrics (gpu__time_duration.sum or equivalent).

Code has been implemented that extracts on-GPU kernel time from NCU output (per-kernel duration summed across profiled kernels) and returns it as both t_ref for the PyTorch baseline and t_best for the candidate implementation.

The measurement path uses NCU-reported on-GPU time exclusively, and does not fall back to Python-level torch.cuda.Event or wall-clock timers for reported speedups (unlike the Sakana AI comparison baseline which uses averaged CUDA-event wall-clock over 2000 runs).
CUTLASS 3.x is installed in the container and reachable by both the SM90+ CollectiveBuilder emission path and the SM70-89 cutlass_cppgen Python emission path.
CUTLASS 3.x headers are present at a known include path, and a smoke test compiles a minimal CollectiveBuilder-based SM90a GEMM instantiation against those headers with nvcc.
The CUTLASS Python API (cutlass_cppgen) is importable from Python and can emit C++ for a Gemm plan (`cutlass.op.Gemm(...).emit()`), covering the SM70-89 and convolution paths used by µCUTLASS.
cutlass_cppgen is extended so that Epilogue Visitor Tree (EVT) chains for SM90a fused epilogues are emitted directly as C++, rather than left unimplemented as in the stock cutlass_cppgen flow.

Code has been implemented that patches / extends cutlass_cppgen to accept an EVT epilogue plan (e.g., evt.chain(bias(), gelu(), clip(...))) and emit corresponding C++ epilogue visitor code compilable with CUTLASS 3.x.

The emitted CUTLASS C++ code (including EVT epilogue) is written into a wrapper header `ucutlass_<hash>.h` placed in a deterministic namespace derived from sha256 of the config, and the original µCUTLASS source is embedded as a comment for traceability.
The OpenHands agent runtime is installed and configured to drive multi-turn kernel optimization in a per-problem workspace, with a custom µCUTLASS compilation tool exposed to the agent.
The OpenHands runtime package is installed in the container and can be launched programmatically for a given problem workspace with the configured GPT-5-mini / GPT-5 / GPT-5.2 backend.
The OpenHands agent is started with its file-editing tools enabled so it can iteratively edit cuda_model.cu (and related files) across turns within a single per-problem workspace.

For variants with µCUTLASS enabled, a custom tool named `ucutlass_compile` is registered with the OpenHands agent that accepts a µCUTLASS DSL string, invokes the compiler, and writes the generated `ucutlass_*.h` header into the workspace where cuda_model.cu can #include it.

The 59-problem KernelBench evaluation subset (spanning Levels 1–3, selected for modern LLM workloads and excluding IDs 24 and 80) is prepared with the reference PyTorch implementations for each problem.
The KernelBench source dataset (250 GPU kernel problems across Levels 1–3) is acquired and made accessible to the pipeline as the raw pool from which the 59-problem subset is drawn.
Code has been implemented to fetch/vendor the upstream KernelBench dataset (Ouyang et al., 2025) into the workspace and expose a consistent path root for Levels 1, 2, and 3 problem folders.
Code has been implemented that can enumerate all 250 KernelBench problems by (level, problem_id) tuples, so that the subset selector operates over the full pool rather than a preselected slice.
A machine-readable manifest defines the 59-problem evaluation subset, encoding the Level/ID inclusion list and the two documented exclusions from Section 5.2 / Footnote 2 / Appendix A.3.
Code has been implemented that emits a subset manifest file (e.g., kernelbench_subset.json/yaml) enumerating each selected problem with at least fields for `level` (1|2|3) and `problem_id` (integer).

Code has been implemented for the subset selector that applies the paper's inclusion rule (problems representative of Transformers, SSMs, and modern recurrent models from Qwen-2.5-7B, Mistral-7B, Phi-3.5-mini, Mamba, RWKV profiling) and explicitly drops Level 2 IDs 24 and 80.
The subset manifest contains exactly 59 problems, matching the paper's stated evaluation size.
The subset manifest contains problems from all three KernelBench levels (Level 1, Level 2, and Level 3 each have ≥1 entry), matching the Levels 1–3 span claimed in Section 5.2.
No entry in the subset manifest has (level=2, problem_id=80) — the GemmMaxSubtractGELU problem excluded per Section 4.4 and Section 5.2 for admitting a zero-output shortcut.
No entry in the subset manifest has (level=2, problem_id=24) — the second Level 2 problem excluded in Section 5.2 for admitting an unintended shortcut implementation.

The subset manifest's Level 3 entries include the LLM-architecture problems named in Appendix A.3 (e.g., MLP variants 1/2/3, causal attention block 43, GPT block 44, Mamba SSM 48 and 49, ReLU self-attention 50).

The subset manifest's Level 2 entries include the fused-op problems named in Appendix A.3 (e.g., IDs 9, 28, 29, 37, 40, 41, 53, 56, 59, 62, 63, 66, 70, 76, 81, 86, 88, 94, 97, 99), matching the paper's LLM-workload rationale.

A rationale document is emitted alongside the manifest that records the profiling-driven selection basis (Qwen-2.5-7B, Mistral-7B, Phi-3.5-mini, Mamba, RWKV) and the explicit exclusion of pooling and legacy CV/RNN tasks, mirroring Footnote 2.
Each of the 59 selected problems is materialized in a per-problem workspace together with its unmodified reference PyTorch implementation, ready for use as the correctness/PyTorch-baseline reference.

Code has been implemented that, for every (level, problem_id) in the subset manifest, copies the upstream KernelBench reference Python file (containing the `Model` class) into that problem's workspace at a predictable path (e.g., `problems/L{level}/p{id}/model.py`).

Code has been implemented so that each per-problem reference module exposes the KernelBench-standard `get_inputs()` and `get_init_inputs()` (or equivalent) entry points, and importing the module does not perform any modification of the reference tensors/parameters.

Code has been implemented that, for each of the 59 problems, instantiates the reference `Model`, runs a forward pass with `get_inputs()` on the target CUDA device, and confirms it returns finite FP32 tensor(s) of the expected shape — establishing the reference is executable end-to-end.

A subset-loader API is implemented that yields, for each of the 59 subset entries, a triple `(level, problem_id, reference_module)` consumable by the downstream bootstrap harness so subsequent stages (SOL analysis, PyTorch baseline profiling, agent workspace seeding) all iterate over the same 59 problems.

A per-problem workspace with driver.cpp, cuda_model.cu seed delegating to PyTorch, Makefile with compile/run/profile targets, PyTorch baseline profiling (t_ref) via NCU, and SOL report generation once at bootstrap is implemented.
The bootstrapper prepares a self-contained per-problem workspace containing the driver, model seed file, and build configuration necessary for the Generate-Compile-Test-Profile loop.
Code has been implemented that creates a per-problem workspace containing a driver.cpp file (the C++ test driver) for each KernelBench problem in the evaluation subset.
Code has been implemented that creates a cuda_model.cu file exposing a `kernel_impl` function that is called by the driver; the body of `kernel_impl` is defined in cuda_model.cu.

The seed cuda_model.cu written at bootstrap initially delegates the `kernel_impl` computation to PyTorch (the PyTorch fallback), providing a functional baseline that the agent later replaces with an optimized CUDA kernel.
Each per-problem workspace is self-contained (isolated directory per KernelBench problem ID) so that agent variants operate independently without cross-problem file contamination.
A Makefile provides compile, run, and profile targets that build cuda_model.cu against driver.cpp and support Nsight Compute (NCU) profiling of the resulting binary.
Code has been implemented that provides a Makefile compile target which builds driver.cpp together with cuda_model.cu into an executable binary for the per-problem workspace.
Code has been implemented that provides a Makefile run target which executes the compiled driver binary to perform the correctness comparison against the PyTorch reference.
Code has been implemented that provides a Makefile profile target which invokes NVIDIA Nsight Compute (NCU) on the driver binary to collect on-GPU kernel execution time measurements.
The driver.cpp calls the agent's kernel_impl, compares its output against the PyTorch reference, and supports NCU profiling of the kernel under test.
Code has been implemented so that driver.cpp invokes the `kernel_impl` function (whose body lives in cuda_model.cu) to produce the candidate kernel output.
The driver compares the kernel_impl output against the PyTorch reference output for numerical correctness before profiling is performed, so incorrect kernels are rejected by the harness.

The driver supports NCU profiling such that the `profile` target can measure on-GPU kernel execution time while excluding kernel launch overhead, host-device synchronization, and Python framework latency.
The bootstrapper profiles the PyTorch baseline via NCU once per problem to establish the reference runtime t_ref used for downstream speedup computations.
Code has been implemented that, during bootstrap, runs the seed (PyTorch-delegating) cuda_model.cu through the profile target to record a per-problem PyTorch baseline reference runtime t_ref.

The recorded t_ref values are the NCU-reported on-GPU kernel execution times (not wall-clock CUDA event times) for the PyTorch baseline, and are persisted per problem so agent variants can compute speedups relative to them.
A Speed-of-Light (SOL) report is generated once at bootstrap per problem and reused across all agent variant experiments, produced under an FP32 problem formulation with TF32 throughput assumptions.
Code has been implemented so that the bootstrapper generates the SOL report exactly once per KernelBench problem during bootstrap, rather than regenerating it per attempt or per agent variant.

The bootstrap-generated SOL report (containing t_SOL and structured problem characterization) is stored in the per-problem workspace and reused across all agent variants (MI baseline, µCUTLASS+MI, in-prompt and orchestrated SOL-guided variants), matching the paper's claim that the SOL report depends only on the problem specification and is reused across variants.

For optimization steering, the bootstrap SOL report is produced by an LLM under an FP32 problem formulation with TF32 throughput assumptions (as stated in Section 5.4 / 4.1), so t_SOL values used by the steering agent reflect the FP32/TF32 ceiling rather than the FP16 ceiling.

The µCUTLASS DSL is implemented as a compact grammar (~170 line EBNF) with a Python CLI compiler that parses, lowers to a typed configuration IR, statically validates constraints (architecture gating, alignment, layout, scheduler/stages, op-specific), and emits CUTLASS C++ (SM90+ CollectiveBuilder) or routes via cutlass_cppgen (SM70–89) into a deterministic-namespace ucutlass_hash.h header with PyTorch driver.
The µCUTLASS EBNF grammar is implemented as a compact Lark-style specification covering kernel configuration, epilogue fusion, and pipeline productions with constraint annotations.
Code has been implemented that ships a grammar file (e.g., grammar.lark or equivalent EBNF specification) inside the µCUTLASS compiler package and loads it at import time as the frontend parser.
The grammar's non-comment production body is approximately 170 lines, matching the paper's claim about EBNF specification size including constraint annotations.

Code has been implemented so the grammar contains productions for the top-level operator entrypoints (gemm(), grouped_gemm, conv2d, conv3d, conv1d, depthwise_conv, grouped_conv) that appear in Table 1's coverage row.

The grammar defines an epilogue-chain production that binds the `>>` operator as a left-associative composition of epilogue nodes so that expressions like `gemm(...) >> bias() >> gelu() >> clip(min=0, max=6)` parse into a chain.
The grammar defines a `pipeline(...)` production that accepts an ordered list of stage sub-expressions and models explicit kernel boundaries between them.
Code has been implemented so the grammar exposes chainable `.with_*` method call productions that carry structured arguments (kwargs) into the IR without requiring positional-only calls.

The GEMM example from Figure 1 (`gemm().with_dtype(...).with_layout(...).with_arch(sm90a).with_threadblockshape(...).with_stages(2).with_alignment(...).with_scheduler(...) >> bias() >> gelu() >> clip(min=0, max=6)`) parses without errors to a full parse tree covering every method call and epilogue node.
The µCUTLASS compiler is exposed as a Python CLI that supports file-based and text-string input modes and is wired as an agent-callable tool.
Code has been implemented that installs a standalone Python CLI entrypoint (e.g., `python -m ucutlass` or a console_scripts entry) for invoking the compiler from the shell.
The CLI accepts a file path to a `kernel.dsl` program and compiles the file end-to-end into the generated header artifact.
The CLI accepts a DSL program as a text string (tool-oriented mode), so the compiler can be invoked without a materialized file on disk.

Code has been implemented so a `ucutlass_compile` tool wrapper is registered with the OpenHands/agent runtime and forwards a DSL string to the compiler, then writes a `ucutlass_*.h` header into the agent workspace.

The compiler pipeline in code follows the parse → lower → validate → emit sequence with distinct functions/classes for each phase (parser stage, IR lowering, validator, emitter) so intermediate stages are testable.
When validation fails the compiler exits with a non-zero return code and prints an explanatory diagnostic (naming the offending field or constraint) rather than silently emitting a header.
Parsed programs are lowered into a typed configuration IR with named dataclasses covering the operation, its data/layout/arch parameters, and any epilogue or pipeline composition.
Code has been implemented that defines a `KernelConfig` (or equivalently named) typed dataclass holding all `.with_*` decisions for a single-kernel program.
Code has been implemented that defines a `PipelineConfig` (or equivalently named) typed dataclass composing an ordered list of stage KernelConfigs from a `pipeline(...)` program.
The IR represents the epilogue chain as an ordered sequence of typed epilogue-node objects (with names such as bias, gelu, clip, custom, etc.) attached to the KernelConfig.

The KernelConfig IR carries explicit fields for dtype (input/acc/output), layout (A/B/C), arch (SM level), alignment (per-operand), and stages, so downstream validation and emission read named attributes rather than raw dictionaries.
The KernelConfig IR carries explicit fields for both SM70–89-style tile / swizzle / iterator / split_k choices and SM90+-style threadblockshape / cluster / scheduler choices.
The IR provides a serialization/`repr` path that can round-trip a KernelConfig to a canonical string used both for the DSL comment in the emitted header and for the namespace hash input.

The compiler statically validates the IR against architecture gating, alignment, layout, scheduler/stages, and operator-specific constraints before invoking any code-emission backend, producing explanatory errors on failure.
The validator has a centralized architecture-gating step that reads the KernelConfig's `arch` field (e.g., sm70, sm80, sm90, sm90a) and rejects features whose SM range excludes the target.
The validator gates `.with_threadblockshape`, `.with_cluster`, and `.with_scheduler` to SM90+ targets and rejects them for SM70–89 configurations, per Table 1(b).
The validator gates `.with_tile`, `.with_swizzle`, `.with_iterator`, and `.with_split_k` to SM70–89 targets and rejects them for SM90+ configurations, per Table 1(b).
The validator rejects `custom(...)` epilogue expressions on any target other than SM90a, matching Table 1(c)'s footnote †.
The validator rejects Conv3d wgrad on SM90+ targets, per Table 1(a) which lists Conv3d wgrad as SM70–89 with an explicit SM90+ cross.
The validator enforces the `.with_operand_swap(true)` precondition that the operation is SM90+ FP32 GEMM with M = N, and errors when the shape is asymmetric.
The validator checks per-operand alignment values from `.with_alignment(...)` against the chosen dtype and layout and rejects unsupported alignments before emission.
The validator constrains layouts to the operator's supported set (NHWC for Conv2d, NDHWC for Conv3d, RowMajor/ColMajor combinations for GEMM) and rejects any other layout for those operators.
The validator enforces that `.with_stages(...)` is a positive integer within the range supported by the chosen scheduler and architecture, rejecting mismatched combinations.

The validator routes depthwise convolutions on SM90+ through a CuTe-based backend with additional restrictions (limited stride/dilation and epilogue support) and rejects unsupported combinations for SM70–89 depthwise conv, per Table 1(a) footnote *.
For Conv1d programs, the lowering step lifts the input to a Conv2d configuration with H = 1 and preserves the semantics through validation.

On validation failure the compiler produces a diagnostic that names the offending field and the constraint that was violated, matching the paper's claim that error messages 'explain what went wrong and why' so the model can fix the DSL before a compile/run/profile attempt.
Validation is invoked before any C++ / CUTLASS toolchain call (no `cutlass_cppgen`, `nvcc`, or CollectiveBuilder header write happens on an invalid IR).

The compiler routes well-formed IR to the correct code-emission backend (SM90+ CollectiveBuilder directly, SM70–89 and convolutions via cutlass_cppgen), with EVT support for SM90+ epilogue chains and multi-stage drivers for pipeline programs.

For SM90+ GEMM configurations, the emitter writes C++ that instantiates the CUTLASS 3.x CollectiveBuilder API (e.g., `cutlass::gemm::device::GemmUniversalAdapter<...>`) directly, without going through cutlass_cppgen.
For SM70–89 operations and for all convolutions, the emitter routes through the CUTLASS Python API (`cutlass_cppgen`) to produce the C++ kernel code.
The cutlass_cppgen flow emits an intermediate `kernel.py` plan file that constructs a `cutlass.op.Gemm(...)` (or equivalent) object and attaches the epilogue chain before calling `plan.emit()`.
Code has been implemented that invokes `cutlass_cppgen` on the emitted plan and produces a `kernel.cu` file, then wraps its contents into the final `ucutlass_<hash>.h` header.
For SM90+ programs, the emitter fuses a chain of epilogue nodes into a single Epilogue Visitor Tree (EVT) rather than a sequence of separate epilogues.

The codebase includes an extension of `cutlass_cppgen` (patch, subclass, or vendored fork) that adds direct C++ emission for EVT expressions, since the default `cutlass_cppgen` flow does not emit C++ for EVT.

`pipeline(...)` programs compile to a multi-stage driver that runs explicit transform stages (layout transposes fused with dtype conversion), then the main kernel stage, then optional inverse transforms back to the original layout/dtype.
The pipeline transform stages are emitted as CUTLASS/CUDA code that performs layout transpose and dtype conversion together in one kernel (rather than two separate kernels).

Emission is dispatched from a single routing function that takes the validated IR and selects the correct backend (SM90+ CollectiveBuilder, SM70–89 cutlass_cppgen, depthwise CuTe SM90+) so backends stay decoupled.

The emitted header includes the required CUTLASS includes and type aliases (e.g., `using DeviceKernel = cutlass::gemm::device::GemmUniversalAdapter<...>;`) matching the shape shown in Figure 1's generated `kernel.cu` snippet.

The emitted C++ artifact is a `ucutlass_<hash>.h` header placed in a deterministic namespace derived from the configuration hash, with the original DSL source embedded as a comment for traceability and cache reuse.
The compiler names its emitted header `ucutlass_<hash>.h` (where <hash> is a deterministic digest of the configuration), matching the naming convention shown in Figure 1.
The `<hash>` value is computed by SHA-256 (or the sha256 helper referenced by Figure 1's `sha256(config) → ucutlass_hash`) applied to the canonical serialization of the KernelConfig / PipelineConfig.

The header wraps its generated aliases and entrypoints inside `namespace ucutlass_<hash> { ... }` so that multiple compiled configurations can coexist in the same translation unit without symbol collisions.
The emitter embeds the original µCUTLASS source program as a `/* Original DSL: ... */` comment block inside the generated header for traceability.
The compiler reuses the existing header (short-circuiting emission) when a subsequent invocation produces the same configuration hash, enabling the caching claim in Section 3.
The hash is deterministic across separate CLI invocations on the same DSL program (invariant to Python dict ordering / process randomness), enabling reliable cross-attempt comparisons.

The emitted header exposes a PyTorch-compatible driver (`kernel(...)` entrypoint) that packs strides, builds kernel arguments, allocates workspace, dispatches on the current PyTorch CUDA stream, and returns the output tensor.

The header declares a top-level entrypoint (e.g., `at::Tensor kernel(A, B, /*C*/, alpha, beta)`) that is callable from the driver.cpp / cuda_model.cu integration and matches Figure 1's wrapper signature.
The driver wrapper packs input tensor strides into the CUTLASS argument structure so that non-contiguous or transposed tensors are handled correctly.
The driver wrapper builds the CUTLASS `Arguments` object (with pointers, extents, alpha, beta, and epilogue params) before launching the kernel.
The driver wrapper queries the CUTLASS workspace size, allocates it via `at::empty` (or equivalent CUDA-backed allocator), and passes the pointer into the launch.
The driver wrapper launches the CUTLASS kernel on the current PyTorch CUDA stream (via `at::cuda::getCurrentCUDAStream()` or equivalent) rather than the default stream.
The driver wrapper returns the output tensor (allocated if not supplied by the caller) so the `kernel_impl` symbol used by driver.cpp can compare it against the PyTorch reference.

End-to-end behavioral checks confirm that the parse→lower→validate→emit pipeline actually rejects invalid programs, produces a compilable C++ artifact for well-formed programs, and integrates numerically with PyTorch.

A syntactically valid but constraint-violating program (e.g., `custom(...)` epilogue on SM80) is rejected by the validator and produces no header on disk, demonstrating that invalid configurations are 'statically ruled out early, rather than at runtime'.
The compiler compiles Figure 1's SM90a GEMM+bias+gelu+clip example end-to-end (parse→lower→validate→emit) to a `ucutlass_<hash>.h` header without errors.

The emitted header from the Figure 1 example compiles cleanly against the installed CUTLASS 3.x headers with `nvcc` targeting SM90a (no undefined symbols or template errors), demonstrating that the emission actually produces valid CUTLASS C++.

A compiled GEMM kernel (e.g., FP16 in / FP32 acc / FP16 out with bias+gelu+clip) produces output tensors that match a PyTorch reference within numerical tolerance when driven through the emitted wrapper, matching the paper's claim that examples 'check correctness against PyTorch references'.

A SM70–89 target program (e.g., an Ampere GEMM with `.with_tile`, `.with_stages`, `.with_swizzle`) is routed through the cutlass_cppgen backend, producing an emitted `kernel.py` plan file, a `kernel.cu` artifact, and a final wrapped `ucutlass_<hash>.h`.

A `pipeline(...)` program with a transpose+dtype-conversion pre-stage, a main GEMM stage, and an inverse transpose+dtype-conversion post-stage compiles end-to-end into a multi-stage driver whose emitted header launches the three stages in order.

The µCUTLASS DSL exposes .with_dtype/.with_layout/.with_arch/.with_alignment/.with_stages/.with_tile/.with_threadblockshape/.with_cluster/.with_scheduler/.with_swizzle/.with_iterator/.with_split_k/.with_operand_swap bindings; supports epilogue chaining with >> (relu, gelu, silu, sigmoid, tanh, mish, hardswish, leaky_relu, elu, clip, clamp, bias, per-channel/row/col scale, aux_store, aux_load, and custom expressions on SM90a compiled to Epilogue Visitor Trees); and supports pipeline(...) multi-stage kernels where layout transposes are fused with dtype conversion at explicit kernel boundaries.
Kernel configuration bindings (.with_* fluent methods) are implemented on the DSL builder for all documented knobs, with architecture gating enforced during static validation.
Core dtype/layout/arch bindings are implemented for GEMM/conv builders.

Code has been implemented that exposes .with_dtype(input=..., acc=..., output=...) on the DSL builder and threads the selected element types (FP64, FP32, FP16, BF16, FP8 on SM90+, INT8) into the emitted CUTLASS type aliases.
Code has been implemented that exposes .with_layout(A=..., B=..., C=...) accepting RowMajor and ColumnMajor and emits the corresponding CUTLASS layout template parameters.

Code has been implemented that exposes .with_arch(sm70|sm75|sm80|sm86|sm89|sm90|sm90a) and routes the builder to the SM70–89 CUTLASS Python API (cutlass_cppgen) backend or the SM90+ CollectiveBuilder backend based on the selected architecture.
Code has been implemented that exposes .with_alignment(A=..., B=..., C=...) accepting element counts and validates alignment against dtype size and architecture rules during static checks.
Code has been implemented that exposes .with_stages(n) for pipeline depth and passes the integer stage count into the CUTLASS template instantiation for all supported architectures (SM70+).
Architecture-gated shape and scheduler bindings are implemented and validated per-arch.
Code has been implemented that exposes .with_tile(m, n, k) for SM70–89 targets and rejects tile shapes that violate CUTLASS 2.x tiling constraints before code emission.
Code has been implemented that exposes .with_threadblockshape(m, n, k) exclusively for SM90+ targets and raises a static validation error if used with an SM70–89 arch.
Code has been implemented that exposes .with_cluster(x, y, z) for SM90+ CTA cluster shape configuration and threads the cluster shape into the CollectiveBuilder call.

Code has been implemented that exposes .with_scheduler(kernel=..., epilogue=...) accepting tma/warp-specialized/cooperative/pingpong style scheduler names on SM90+ and rejects unsupported combinations.
Code has been implemented that exposes .with_swizzle(...) for SM70–89 GEMMs and emits the corresponding threadblock swizzle template argument.
Conv-specific and specialty bindings are implemented and gated to the correct operator families.
Code has been implemented that exposes .with_iterator(...) on conv builders (SM70–89) to select the CUTLASS conv iterator algorithm (e.g., analytic, optimized) and rejects it on GEMM builders.
Code has been implemented that exposes .with_split_k(n) on SM70–89 conv builders and emits the corresponding split-K slicing argument into the generated kernel.

Code has been implemented that exposes .with_operand_swap(true) for SM90+ FP32 GEMMs and validates the M == N requirement documented in Table 1, rejecting non-square problem shapes at parse/lower time.
Static validation rejects invalid binding combinations before invoking the CUTLASS toolchain.

The DSL compiler reports a structured validation error (naming the offending binding) when an SM90+-only binding such as .with_threadblockshape or .with_cluster is combined with an SM70–89 architecture selector, without invoking nvcc.
The DSL compiler reports an alignment validation error when .with_alignment specifies element counts incompatible with the selected dtype and architecture, before emitting any C++ code.
The DSL compiler rejects a .with_operand_swap(true) specification on an SM90+ FP32 GEMM where M != N with an explanatory error citing the M == N constraint.
Epilogue fusion via the `>>` chaining operator is implemented across all documented built-in operations and, on SM90a, custom expressions compiled to Epilogue Visitor Trees (EVT).
The `>>` operator overload composes epilogue nodes into a chain that lowers to a single fused CUTLASS epilogue.

Code has been implemented that defines a Python `__rshift__` (or equivalent) on the kernel/epilogue builder so that `gemm() >> bias() >> gelu() >> clip(min=0, max=6)` parses without error and produces an ordered epilogue chain object.

A chained epilogue expression compiles to a single fused CUTLASS epilogue instantiation (verified by inspecting the emitted C++ containing exactly one epilogue functor/EVT rather than a sequence of independent epilogue calls).
Built-in activation epilogues are implemented and route to the correct CUTLASS/EVT primitives.
Code has been implemented that exposes `relu()`, `gelu()`, `silu()`, `sigmoid()`, `tanh()`, `mish()`, `hardswish()`, `leaky_relu(alpha=...)`, and `elu(alpha=...)` as chainable epilogue nodes.
Each built-in activation epilogue emits the correct CUTLASS activation functor (e.g., cutlass::epilogue::thread::ReLu, GELU, SiLu) in the generated C++ when the DSL program targets SM70–89.

A driver that runs a compiled GEMM with an epilogue chain including a built-in activation (e.g., `gemm() >> gelu()`) produces outputs within FP16/FP32 tolerance of the corresponding PyTorch reference (torch.matmul followed by torch.nn.functional.gelu) on a small test problem.
Clamping and bias/scale epilogues are implemented.
Code has been implemented that exposes `clip(min=..., max=...)` and `clamp(min=..., max=...)` epilogue nodes with min/max parameters passed through to the generated CUTLASS clamp functor.
Code has been implemented that exposes a `bias()` epilogue node which wires a per-output bias tensor into the epilogue functor and into the kernel launch argument struct.

sub_tasks.requirements: The SOL analysis module implements problem characterization (operators, dims, dtypes, FLOPs, best-case DRAM bytes with fusion of intermediates), hardware limits (peak compute and BW scaled by current clocks from nvidia-smi with 1500 MHz default), roofline bounds computing arithmetic intensity, T_compute, T_mem, t_SOL = max(...), and compute-vs-memory bottleneck classification via ridge-point comparison; produces both an FP32/TF32 report (for steering) and an FP16-based tighter report (for scheduling and integrity).

Problem characterization identifies operators, tensor dimensions, and data types from the reference model, and estimates total FLOPs and best-case DRAM bytes assuming each unique input element is read once and each output is written once, with intermediates fused where feasible.
Code has been implemented to parse the reference computation (single operator or multi-operator graph) and enumerate the operators together with their tensor dimensions and data types.
Code has been implemented to compute total FLOPs for each identified operator based on its dimensions (e.g., 2*M*N*K for a GEMM).
Code has been implemented to compute best-case DRAM bytes under the assumption that each unique input element is read exactly once and each output element is written exactly once.
The DRAM-bytes calculation fuses intermediates where feasible: intermediate tensors produced and consumed within the graph do not contribute to DRAM traffic in the best-case bytes estimate.
Behavioral test: FLOPs computed for a plain (M, N, K) GEMM equals 2*M*N*K, matching the standard roofline convention.
Behavioral test: for a fused GEMM+bias+activation operator sequence, computed DRAM bytes exclude the materialization of the intermediate GEMM output (fusion of intermediates is honored).

Hardware limits derive peak compute throughput and peak memory bandwidth from H100 (SM90a) published specifications, scaled by the current GPU clock frequency reported by nvidia-smi, with a default of 1500 MHz when the query is unavailable.
Code has been implemented to query current GPU clock frequencies (SM/graphics clock) from nvidia-smi and parse the result into a numeric MHz value.
Code has been implemented to fall back to a default clock frequency of 1500 MHz when nvidia-smi output is unavailable or cannot be parsed.
Code stores published H100 SM90a peak compute throughput values (per relevant precision including FP32/TF32 and FP16/BF16) that the roofline model can look up.
Code stores published H100 SM90a peak DRAM/HBM bandwidth used as the memory-side roofline ceiling.
Behavioral test: peak compute throughput is scaled proportionally to the current clock frequency (e.g., halving the clock halves the compute ceiling).
The roofline bound computes arithmetic intensity, T_compute, T_mem, and t_SOL = max(T_compute, T_mem) from the characterized FLOPs/bytes and the hardware limits.
Code has been implemented to compute arithmetic intensity as FLOPs divided by DRAM bytes.
Code has been implemented to compute T_compute = FLOPs / Peak FLOP/s using the (clock-scaled) compute ceiling.
Code has been implemented to compute T_mem = Bytes / Peak BW using the (clock-scaled) memory bandwidth ceiling.
Code has been implemented to compute the SOL lower-bound runtime as t_SOL = max(T_compute, T_mem).
Behavioral test: for a synthetic problem whose arithmetic intensity is well above the ridge point, t_SOL equals T_compute (and equals T_mem in the memory-bound regime).
Bottleneck classification compares the arithmetic intensity to the ridge point (Peak FLOP/s divided by Peak BW) and labels each problem as compute-bound or memory-bound.
Code has been implemented to compute the ridge point as Peak FLOP/s divided by Peak BW under the current hardware-limits configuration.
Code emits a bottleneck-classification label of 'compute-bound' when arithmetic intensity >= ridge point and 'memory-bound' otherwise.

Behavioral test: a low-arithmetic-intensity elementwise operator (e.g., a simple activation or add) is classified as memory-bound, and a large square GEMM at compute-friendly dimensions is classified as compute-bound.

The FP32/TF32 SOL report is generated (per Section 4.1 and Appendix A.2) under an FP32 problem formulation with TF32 throughput assumptions and is used as the steering signal (SOL gap g = t_best / t_SOL).

Code has been implemented to produce a structured SOL report (operators, FLOPs, DRAM bytes, arithmetic intensity, T_compute, T_mem, t_SOL, bottleneck) via an LLM-based generator (with an analytical fallback allowed).
The steering-report generator uses TF32 throughput values from the peak-compute table when computing T_compute for FP32-specified KernelBench problems.

The emitted report structure matches the schema exemplified in Appendix A.2 (compact structured fields covering problem characterization, hardware limits, roofline bound, and bottleneck classification).
Code has been implemented so the SOL report is computed once during per-problem bootstrap and reused across all subsequent agent attempts/iterations rather than regenerated per attempt.
Downstream code exposes the FP32/TF32 t_SOL to the steering workflow such that the SOL gap g = t_best / t_SOL (used in the ROI ranking) can be computed from the report.
The FP16-based SOL report provides a tighter runtime ceiling for scheduling and integrity checking, using FP16 peak throughput while preserving FP32 I/O sizes when computing DRAM bytes.
Code has been implemented to generate an FP16-based SOL report that substitutes FP16 (or BF16) peak compute throughput into T_compute.
The FP16-based report continues to treat inputs and outputs as FP32 (as allocated by KernelBench) when computing DRAM bytes; only the compute-side precision is changed.
Behavioral test: for a compute-bound GEMM, the FP16-based t_SOL is strictly tighter (smaller) than the FP32/TF32-based t_SOL under the same problem specification.

The FP16-based t_SOL is exposed through an interface consumed by the SOL-guided budget scheduler and the SOL-ceiling integrity detector (i.e., it is the ceiling used for scheduling and integrity, not the FP32/TF32 report).
The SOL analysis pipeline produces valid FP32/TF32 and FP16 reports across the 59-problem evaluation subset and exhibits documented modeling caveats consistent with the paper.

Both the FP32/TF32 and FP16 SOL reports are successfully generated for all 59 problems in the KernelBench evaluation subset (no missing reports required to run steering, scheduling, and integrity checks).
Code documents (in comments or the emitted report metadata) that sparsity exploitation is not modeled and perfect caching is assumed, per the caveats stated in Section 4.1.

Measured: for a representative KernelBench Level 1 GEMM problem, the FP32/TF32 t_SOL matches the analytical value derived from FLOPs/(TF32 peak at 1500 MHz) within a small tolerance, confirming the roofline arithmetic is calibrated to the paper's hardware assumptions.

The flat Measure–Implement (MI) controller drives a Generate–Compile–Test–Profile loop within OpenHands, with a per-problem attempt budget of 40 attempts (each attempt allowing a fixed number of internal turns), the ucutlass_compile custom tool integrated when µCUTLASS is enabled, and lightweight context management passing forward only limited information between attempts.
The MI controller implements the flat Generate–Compile–Test–Profile loop that constitutes a single attempt, invoking the bootstrap workspace's toolchain for each phase.

Code has been implemented that defines an MI controller entry point (e.g., a function/class such as `run_mi_controller` or equivalent) which orchestrates a per-attempt Generate–Compile–Test–Profile loop for one KernelBench problem.

The Generate step of the loop causes the agent (via OpenHands) to edit `cuda_model.cu` (and, when applicable, the µCUTLASS DSL source) inside the per-problem workspace before the compile step is invoked.
The Compile step invokes the workspace Makefile's compile target (building the candidate `cuda_model.cu` plus `driver.cpp`) and surfaces build errors back to the agent for the next turn/attempt.

The Test step runs the compiled driver, which compares `kernel_impl` output against the PyTorch reference and reports pass/fail; failed correctness gates the attempt from being counted as a valid speedup candidate.

The Profile step invokes NVIDIA Nsight Compute (`ncu`) via the Makefile profile target on the correct kernel and records the reported on-GPU kernel time as the candidate's `t_best` measurement for that attempt.

The controller enforces the attempt/turn hierarchy: each attempt is one pass through Generate–Compile–Test–Profile with a fixed internal turn budget, and the per-problem attempt budget matches Table 2.
Code has been implemented that treats one pass through the Generate–Compile–Test–Profile loop as exactly one 'attempt' and increments a persistent attempt counter accordingly.

Within a single attempt, the controller allows the LLM a configurable, fixed number of internal turns (LLM interactions with file-editing/tool calls) before the compile+evaluate sequence is triggered.
The controller terminates the per-problem run once the attempt counter reaches the configured budget (default 40 for MI variants per Table 2) and does not proceed to a 41st attempt.
The MI variant configuration exposes 'total attempts' as a parameter set to 40 for both `MI w/o µCUTLASS` and `MI + µCUTLASS`, matching the values in Table 2.
OpenHands is used as the agent runtime, providing per-problem workspace and file-editing tools that the MI controller uses to execute multi-turn attempts.
Code has been implemented that launches an OpenHands agent runtime session (or an equivalent OpenHands-based executor) to host the MI controller's multi-turn LLM interactions.

The OpenHands session is scoped to the per-problem bootstrap workspace (containing `driver.cpp`, `cuda_model.cu`, and the Makefile) so that all file edits and tool invocations occur within that problem's directory.
OpenHands' built-in file-editing tools (read/write/edit) are exposed to the agent so that it can modify `cuda_model.cu` (and DSL sources in µCUTLASS variants) across turns within an attempt.
The MI controller's system/user prompt instructs the agent that its task is to edit `cuda_model.cu`, replacing the PyTorch fallback with an optimized custom kernel implementation.
The `ucutlass_compile` custom tool is registered with the OpenHands agent for µCUTLASS-enabled variants and integrates the DSL compiler into the attempt loop.
Code has been implemented that registers a custom OpenHands tool named `ucutlass_compile` and exposes it to the agent only when the µCUTLASS variant flag is enabled.
The `ucutlass_compile` tool accepts a µCUTLASS DSL program as a text-string argument (tool-oriented mode of the DSL compiler) and returns compile status plus error messages back to the agent.

On successful compile, `ucutlass_compile` writes a generated header named `ucutlass_<hash>.h` (deterministic hash of the DSL config) into the per-problem workspace so that `cuda_model.cu` can `#include` it.
For non-µCUTLASS MI variants, the `ucutlass_compile` tool is not registered/available to the agent, so agent traces for those variants contain no invocations of that tool.
Lightweight context management passes forward only limited information between attempts, rather than the full prior transcript.

Code has been implemented that constructs each new attempt's prompt by including only a bounded, curated set of prior-attempt information (e.g., best-so-far kernel summary, latest measurements, error digest) instead of concatenating full transcripts.

The between-attempt context includes the current best correct kernel's measured runtime `t_best` and its speedup over PyTorch `t_ref`, so the agent has continuity of the optimization target across attempts.
The context-management logic does not carry per-turn tool-call histories from earlier attempts verbatim into subsequent attempts, matching the paper's 'lightweight' framing (Section 2.4).
The two MI variants from Table 2 are wired end-to-end with matched per-problem budgets that isolate the effect of code representation.
A `MI w/o µCUTLASS` variant is runnable end-to-end on a KernelBench problem: 40 attempts, no `ucutlass_compile` tool exposed, agent must generate raw CUDA/CUTLASS code in `cuda_model.cu`.

A `MI + µCUTLASS` variant is runnable end-to-end on a KernelBench problem: 40 attempts, `ucutlass_compile` tool exposed, with everything else (turns/attempt, context management, workspace, tools) held constant relative to `MI w/o µCUTLASS`.
The MI-controller wall-time breakdown reported in Section 1 is reproducible from an instrumented single-problem run.

Instrumentation exists that measures, per attempt and totalled across a 40-attempt vanilla MI run on one KernelBench problem, the wall time spent inside LLM calls vs. inside compile+run+profile tool actions, and reports these as fractions of total run time.
On the instrumented single-problem vanilla-MI run, the measured fraction of total time spent in LLM calls matches the paper's reported ≈21% (Section 1) within a reasonable tolerance.

On the same instrumented single-problem vanilla-MI run, the measured fraction of total time spent in compile+run+profile tool actions matches the paper's reported ≈79% (Section 1) within a reasonable tolerance.

MANTIS is implemented in both orchestrated (distinct phases with structured markdown/JSON artifacts) and in-prompt (single MI controller following MANTIS in system prompt) forms; realizes Measure (ncu), Analyze (SOL gap g = t_best/t_SOL and bottleneck attribution), Nominate (hypotheses with causal reasoning), Triage (gap-aware ROI formula with exponent 1 + max(0, log10(g/5)) balancing S_hat, R_impl, R_perf), Implement (Generate-Compile-Test-Profile), and Summarize (with cross-problem persistent memory in the full config); orchestrated variant runs 5 iterations × 2 hypotheses × 4 attempts = 40 total attempts.
Both MANTIS realizations (orchestrated multi-phase controller and in-prompt single-controller) exist as selectable variants sharing common bootstrap artifacts.

Code has been implemented that provides an orchestrated MANTIS controller module distinct from the flat MI controller, exposing separate callable phases (Measure, Analyze, Nominate, Triage, Implement, Summarize).

Code has been implemented that provides an in-prompt MANTIS variant: a single MI controller whose system prompt fully describes the Measure–Analyze–Nominate–Triage–Implement–Summarize methodology and phase responsibilities.

Both MANTIS variants are wired into the same experiment harness/CLI as the MI baseline so any of {MI, MI+µCUTLASS, in-prompt MANTIS, orchestrated MANTIS} × {raw CUDA/CUTLASS, µCUTLASS} can be selected with a single flag.
Both MANTIS variants consume the SOL report produced once by the bootstrap phase rather than regenerating it, and fail loudly if the cached SOL artifact is missing for the problem.
The Measure phase profiles the current best correct kernel and extracts the structured metric summary consumed by Analyze.
Code has been implemented that invokes Nsight Compute (ncu) on the current best correct kernel binary produced by the bootstrap/driver during each Measure step.
The Measure phase parses the ncu output and exposes at minimum occupancy, memory throughput, and compute throughput fields as a structured object consumed by Analyze.
When no correct kernel exists yet (first iteration), Measure returns a well-defined placeholder profile (e.g., using the PyTorch reference or a null summary) rather than crashing the pipeline.
The Analyze phase quantifies the SOL gap and attributes it to bottlenecks by combining the cached SOL report, profiler summary, and current source code.
Code has been implemented that computes the SOL gap as g = t_best / t_SOL, where t_best is the measured best correct kernel time and t_SOL is the LLM-generated FP32/TF32 SOL bound.
Analyze reuses the SOL report produced once during bootstrap across all iterations and variants rather than recomputing it per attempt.
The Analyze prompt/artifact concatenates the Measure profiler summary, the SOL report, and the current best kernel source into a single structured input for downstream reasoning.
The Analyze output includes an explicit bottleneck-attribution field naming the dominant limiter(s) (e.g., memory-bound, compute-bound, launch overhead, occupancy) driving the SOL gap.
The Nominate phase produces multiple candidate optimization hypotheses, each with causal reasoning tied to an analyzed bottleneck and to the SOL gap.
Code has been implemented that generates a list of at least two hypothesis candidates per iteration for use by the Triage phase.
Each nominated hypothesis structured record contains a non-empty causal-reasoning field explaining why the proposal is expected to close the SOL gap.
Each hypothesis explicitly names the analyzed bottleneck(s) it targets, and Triage rejects/downweights hypotheses lacking such an attribution.
Each hypothesis carries numeric estimates for S_hat (expected speedup), R_impl (implementation risk), and R_perf (performance risk) consumed by the Triage ROI formula.
The Triage phase implements the gap-aware ROI formula with exponent 1 + max(0, log10(g/5)) to rank hypotheses and select the top-n for implementation.
Code has been implemented that computes a ROI score per hypothesis as a function of S_hat, R_impl, R_perf, and the current SOL gap g, matching the paper's gap-aware formulation.
The Triage code raises the ambition term to the exponent alpha(g) = 1 + max(0, log10(g/5)), computed with base-10 logarithm and clamped to be ≥ 1.
Behavioral: for any g ≤ 5 the computed gap exponent equals exactly 1.0, so the ROI reduces to the plain S_hat / risk form when the current implementation is already within 5× of SOL.
Behavioral: for g = 50 the computed gap exponent equals 2.0 (since 1 + log10(50/5) = 2), verified via a unit test on the exponent function.
Given two hypotheses with equal risks but different S_hat, Triage's ranking places the higher-S_hat hypothesis strictly above the lower one, and the ranking gap grows with g.
The Triage step selects exactly the top-2 hypotheses per iteration (matching the orchestrated 5×2×4 budget) and passes them to the Implement phase.
Ranking prefers higher-ambition (larger S_hat, higher R) hypotheses when g is large and prefers lower-risk incremental hypotheses when g is small, verified on a small synthetic hypothesis set.
The Implement phase runs a Generate–Compile–Test–Profile inner loop for each selected hypothesis under a fixed per-hypothesis attempt budget.
Code has been implemented that, per selected hypothesis, drives a Generate → Compile → Test → Profile loop reusing the bootstrap workspace's Makefile targets.
Each hypothesis is allocated a fixed budget of exactly 4 attempts in the orchestrated variant, enforced by the controller regardless of intermediate success/failure.
The Implement loop terminates the current hypothesis when its attempt budget is exhausted and returns control to the outer orchestrator, without spilling attempts into other hypotheses.
Each attempt records structured outcome fields (compile success, correctness pass, measured runtime, ncu profile path) so downstream Summarize and integrity checking can consume them.
The Summarize phase reflects on expected-vs-actual outcomes and, in the full MANTIS configuration, persists compact summaries as cross-problem memory retrievable by Nominate.
Code has been implemented that emits a Summarize artifact at the end of each iteration containing a reflection over the evaluated hypotheses.
The Summarize artifact contains explicit expected-vs-actual fields per hypothesis (predicted speedup vs measured speedup, predicted risk vs realized outcome).

The per-iteration summary is bounded in size (compact, distilled lessons) rather than dumping raw per-attempt logs, verified on a run producing summaries that fit within a documented token/character cap.
The full MANTIS configuration writes each iteration's compact summary to a cross-problem memory store keyed such that later problems can retrieve prior summaries.

The Nominate phase, when cross-problem memory is enabled, retrieves the top-k relevant prior summaries and injects them into the hypothesis-generation prompt, and this retrieval path is disabled in the MANTIS-noXmem ablation.
The orchestrated variant executes MANTIS phases as distinct steps with structured markdown/JSON artifacts and matches the 5 × 2 × 4 = 40 attempt budget.
The orchestrated controller runs exactly 5 outer iterations per problem by default (unless SOL-scheduling stops it earlier).

Each MANTIS phase is executed as a distinct LLM call / controller step (not folded into a single prompt), verifiable by inspecting the run trace for phase-labeled boundaries.
The in-prompt variant realizes the MANTIS methodology inside a single MI controller's system prompt while matching the same 40-attempt per-problem budget.
The in-prompt variant's system prompt contains explicit descriptions of all six MANTIS phases (Measure, Analyze, Nominate, Triage, Implement, Summarize) and their responsibilities.

sub_tasks.requirements: A lightweight offline scheduler replays run logs and implements breadth-first round-robin with two eligibility stopping criteria (SOL-headroom threshold ε and no-progress window w) using the FP16 SOL bound, and sweeps ε ∈ {25%, 50%, ..., 300%} and w ∈ {0, 4, 8, 12, 16, 20} independently and jointly to produce token savings and speedup-retention outputs consumable by downstream Pareto and efficiency-gain analyses.

Offline replay infrastructure: the scheduler is a standalone, log-driven module that replays existing per-problem attempt/iteration traces (no live GPU or LLM calls) using a breadth-first round-robin dispatch discipline over eligible problems.

Code has been implemented that provides an offline SOL-guided budget scheduler module (e.g., `sol_scheduler.py` or equivalent) callable from tests/experiments without spawning agents or running kernels.

Code has been implemented that loads per-problem run traces (per-attempt best-so-far runtime, PyTorch reference t_ref, and token/tool cost) from existing logs and exposes them as an in-memory structure the scheduler can iterate over without re-executing agents.

Code has been implemented so that the scheduler advances problems in a breadth-first round-robin order: on each dispatch it picks the next currently-eligible problem in cyclic order and consumes exactly one recorded attempt (or one iteration for orchestrated variants) from its trace before rotating to the next problem.

Code has been implemented so that the scheduler's atomic work-item unit is configurable to either an `attempt` (for MI / in-prompt variants, 40 attempts) or an `iteration` (for orchestrated MANTIS variants, 5 iterations of 2×4 attempts) matching how the original runs were bucketed.

Eligibility stopping criteria: the scheduler implements the SOL-headroom threshold ε rule and the no-progress window w rule described in Section 4.3, both gated on the problem having first surpassed the PyTorch baseline, and supports evaluating them individually or combined (a problem is removed when either fires).
SOL-headroom criterion: the ε rule is implemented as a function that returns 'stop' for a problem when the current best correct kernel time t_best satisfies t_best ≤ (1+ε) · t_SOL.
Code has been implemented that computes, per problem and per replayed attempt, the ratio t_best / t_SOL and evaluates the predicate t_best ≤ (1+ε) · t_SOL for the configured ε.

The ε criterion additionally requires that the problem's current best kernel already beats PyTorch (t_best < t_ref) before the problem can be declared ineligible; otherwise the problem stays eligible even when t_best ≤ (1+ε) · t_SOL is satisfied.
No-progress criterion: the w rule is implemented as a function that returns 'stop' for a problem when its best-so-far speedup has not improved for w consecutive attempts.

Code has been implemented that tracks per-problem the number of consecutive attempts since the last strict improvement in best-so-far speedup over PyTorch and stops the problem once that counter reaches w.

The w criterion additionally requires that the problem has already surpassed PyTorch (t_best < t_ref) at some prior attempt; problems still behind PyTorch continue to receive attempts regardless of how many attempts have elapsed without improvement.
Setting w = 0 disables the no-progress stopping criterion (a value of w = 0 must never trigger a stop by the no-progress rule), consistent with the paper's independent ε sweep at w=0.

Combined eligibility: when both ε and w are enabled the scheduler removes a problem as soon as either criterion fires (logical OR), and never before either fires while the problem is still behind PyTorch.

SOL bound source: budget scheduling uses the tighter FP16-based SOL bound (not the FP32/TF32 estimate used for steering), matching Section 4.1 and Section 5.8's stated policy that FP16 provides a physically tighter ceiling for optimized kernels.
Sweep configuration: the scheduler is exercised over the full ε and w grid described in Section 5.7, both independently and jointly, so that downstream analyses have every (ε, w) policy available.
Code has been implemented that sweeps ε over the set {25%, 50%, 75%, 100%, 125%, 150%, 175%, 200%, 225%, 250%, 275%, 300%} exactly (25% grid from 25% through 300%).
Code has been implemented that sweeps w over the set {0, 4, 8, 12, 16, 20} exactly.
Code has been implemented that runs an independent ε sweep with the no-progress criterion disabled (w = 0), matching Figure 7(a).
Code has been implemented that runs an independent w sweep with ε fixed at 100%, matching Figure 7(b).

Code has been implemented that evaluates the full Cartesian product of ε × w combinations (all 12 × 6 policies) for each variant so a per-variant Pareto frontier of (cost, geomean speedup) can be drawn.

Replay accounting and retention metrics: the scheduler bookkeeping produces the token/attempt costs and speedup-retention numbers required for the Pareto and efficiency-gain analyses, computed strictly from the replayed trace under each policy.

Code has been implemented that, for each (ε, w) policy, sums only the tokens actually consumed up to each problem's stop point (or the full budget if never stopped) to produce a per-policy total token cost, and computes fractional token savings relative to the exhaustive fixed-allocation baseline.
Code has been implemented that similarly aggregates per-policy consumed attempts (or iterations) across the 59 problems and reports fractional attempt savings vs. fixed allocation.

Code has been implemented that, for each (ε, w) policy, uses each problem's best speedup at its stop point (t_ref / t_best_at_stop) to compute both the geomean and median speedup across problems, and reports each as a fraction of the corresponding fixed-allocation geomean/median (`speedup retention`).

Code has been implemented that computes the efficiency gain metric as (g_sched / g_fixed) / (τ_sched / τ_fixed) where g is geomean speedup and τ is total token cost, so that a value above 1× denotes that tokens saved outweigh the speedup lost.

The integrity pipeline implements (1) a SOL-ceiling detector flagging attempts whose measured runtime falls >10% below the FP16 SOL bound, (2) an LLM-based game detector (LGD) that reviews candidate code with reference program, performance context, and SOL report and assigns labels No Issues / Minor Issues / Original Gaming / Inherited Gaming, and (3) a static PyTorch-only detector parsing NCU logs matching against at::native::/cublas/cudnn patterns; produces the accept/reject decision per Section 5.8.

The SOL-ceiling detector implements a strict physical-ceiling check that flags attempts whose measured runtime is faster than expected from first principles, using the FP16-based SOL bound with a small measurement-noise buffer.

Code has been implemented that defines a SOL-ceiling detector module/function which takes as input a candidate attempt's measured on-GPU kernel runtime t_measured and the problem's SOL bound t_SOL and returns a boolean/structured flag indicating whether the attempt violates the ceiling.

Code has been implemented such that the SOL-ceiling detector consumes the FP16-based SOL estimate (tighter FP16 ceiling used for integrity and scheduling, per Section 4.4 / Section 5.8), not the FP32/TF32 steering estimate.

The SOL-ceiling detector uses a violation threshold of exactly 10% below the SOL bound (equivalent to t_measured < 0.9 * t_SOL) as the flag condition, matching the paper's specification of 'more than 10% below the SOL bound'.
Behavioral: an attempt whose measured runtime is greater than or equal to 0.9 * t_SOL (i.e., within the 10% buffer of the SOL ceiling) is NOT flagged by the SOL-ceiling detector.
Behavioral: an attempt whose measured runtime is strictly less than 0.9 * t_SOL is flagged by the SOL-ceiling detector as suspicious/ceiling-violation.
The SOL-ceiling detector emits a structured record (attempt id, t_measured, t_SOL, ratio, flag reason) that is consumable by the downstream accept/reject aggregation stage.

The LLM-based game detector (LGD) reviews each candidate attempt against the reference program plus SOL-derived specification and assigns one of the four labels No Issues / Minor Issues / Original Gaming / Inherited Gaming, with logic to distinguish new exploits from inherited ones.
Code has been implemented for an LGD module/function that invokes an LLM to review a candidate attempt and returns a categorical judgment label.
The LGD prompt includes the candidate kernel source code (cuda_model.cu / uCUTLASS DSL and any generated headers) being reviewed.
The LGD prompt includes the KernelBench reference program (the PyTorch reference module that specifies the intended computation).
The LGD prompt includes performance context for the attempt (measured t_best, PyTorch t_ref, and SOL gap g = t_best / t_SOL).

The LGD prompt includes the structured SOL report (FLOPs, bytes, dominant operators, roofline classification) as specification augmentation so the reviewer can judge whether the candidate performs the intended work.
The LGD output is constrained to and parsed into exactly the label set {No Issues, Minor Issues, Original Gaming, Inherited Gaming}; any other output is rejected or normalized.

Code has been implemented such that when an attempt is judged to be gaming, the LGD (or a wrapper) inspects prior attempts on the same problem and labels the case Inherited Gaming if the same exploit was already present in an earlier attempt, or Original Gaming otherwise.
The LGD parses the LLM's structured (JSON/markdown) response with schema validation and salvage (unknown/misspelled label keys are normalized rather than silently discarded).

Behavioral: on a synthetic candidate matching the Level 2 problem 80 pattern (Gemm-Max-Subtract-GELU collapsing to a zero-write) presented with the correct reference and SOL report, the LGD labels the attempt as Gaming (Original Gaming when no prior attempt exhibits it).

Behavioral: on a benign optimized kernel (e.g., a correct fused GEMM+bias+GELU written in CUDA/CUTLASS) that performs the intended computation, the LGD labels it as No Issues (negative-control check that the detector is not label-happy).

The static PyTorch-only detector parses NCU profile logs, extracts kernel launch signatures, and flags attempts that rely exclusively on PyTorch library kernels (no agent-written custom CUDA/CUTLASS/uCUTLASS kernel).
Code has been implemented for a static PyTorch-only detector that reads the NCU profile log file emitted by the bootstrap harness's `ncu` profiling step.
Code has been implemented that extracts individual kernel launch signatures (kernel names/symbols) from the parsed NCU log.
The detector's library-pattern set includes at minimum the prefixes/patterns `at::native::`, `cublas`, and `cudnn`, matching the paper's stated pattern list.
Behavioral: on an NCU log where every extracted kernel signature matches one of the known library prefixes, the detector flags the attempt as PyTorch-only.

Behavioral: on an NCU log where at least one kernel signature does not match any library pattern (i.e., a user-written custom kernel is present), the detector does NOT flag the attempt as PyTorch-only.

Behavioral: the NCU log parser handles empty, truncated, or otherwise malformed profiler outputs without crashing the integrity pipeline (returns a parse-failure record that the aggregator can act on).

The Section 5.8 aggregation logic combines the three detectors into a single per-attempt accept/reject decision with mutually exclusive category resolution and applies the decision to reported speedup and scheduling results.
Code has been implemented for an integrity pipeline driver that, for each attempt, runs the SOL-ceiling detector, the LGD, and the static PyTorch-only detector and produces a single labeled record.
Behavioral: attempts labeled No Issues or Minor Issues are ACCEPTED by the aggregation logic (retained in reported speedup and scheduling results).
Behavioral: attempts flagged by the SOL-ceiling detector, or labeled Original Gaming, Inherited Gaming, or PyTorch-only are REJECTED (excluded from reported speedup and scheduling results).

Behavioral: when an attempt is flagged by BOTH the LGD (as Gaming) and the static PyTorch-only detector, the aggregation logic classifies it as PyTorch-only, keeping the category set mutually exclusive as specified in Section 5.8.

The integrity pipeline is applied offline (after run completion): flagged/labeled results are computed post-hoc and are NOT fed back to the agent as tool feedback during the Generate-Compile-Test-Profile loop, matching the paper's stated offline application.

Code has been implemented such that when reported speedups (Fast-p, Attempt-Fast-p, geomean/median) and SOL-guided scheduling replays consume run logs, they read the per-attempt integrity label and exclude rejected attempts from both the fixed-budget speedup metrics and offline scheduling eligibility.

Code has been implemented that persists the per-attempt integrity record (SOL-ceiling flag, LGD label with Original/Inherited distinction, PyTorch-only flag, final accept/reject decision) to a per-run artifact (e.g., a JSON/CSV) for downstream reporting and the RQ5 analysis.

The evaluation implements Fast-p(r), Attempt-Fast-p(r) surfaces and the Attempt-Fast-p(2) slice, signed-area computation between Fast-p curves, geomean and median speedup summaries, speedup retention, and the efficiency gain metric (gain relative to fixed-budget geomean/token ratio).
Fast-p(r) curve computation over per-problem best speedups.

Code has been implemented that computes a Fast-p(r) curve from a list of per-problem best speedups over PyTorch, returning, for each speedup threshold r on a user-supplied grid, the fraction (percentage) of problems whose best speedup is ≥ r.

The Fast-p(r) implementation behaves as a complementary CDF: it is monotonically non-increasing in r, evaluates to 100% at r=0, and evaluates at r=1 to the fraction of problems whose best speedup strictly exceeds the PyTorch baseline.

Fast-p plots are generated with the region r ≥ 1 (kernel beats PyTorch) highlighted and use per-variant curves comparable across the four main variants (MI, µCUTLASS+MI, SOL-guided, µCUTLASS+SOL-guided).
Attempt-Fast-p(r) surface and its Attempt-Fast-p(2) slice for optimization efficiency reporting.

Code has been implemented that constructs the Attempt-Fast-p(r) surface: for each (r, a) pair it reports the percentage of problems whose best-so-far speedup across attempts 1..a reaches at least r, where best-so-far is computed as a running maximum of correct attempts per problem.

The Attempt-Fast-p(2) slice fixes the speedup threshold at r=2 and sweeps over attempts 1..A, producing curves used in the right column of Figure 4 to visualize how quickly each variant accumulates ≥2× solutions.
The Attempt-Fast-p computation is monotonically non-decreasing in the attempt index a (best-so-far semantics) and reduces exactly to Fast-p(r) when a equals the full per-problem attempt budget.
Signed-area comparison between two Fast-p curves.

Code has been implemented that computes the signed area ∫[P_A(r) − P_B(r)] dr between two Fast-p curves over a shared r-grid, returning a positive value when curve A dominates and a negative value when curve B dominates.

The signed-area implementation is verified (e.g., by unit test on synthetic per-problem speedup vectors) to equal the difference in arithmetic mean speedups between the two variants, matching the property stated in Section 5.6.

Signed-area values are reported for the orchestrated-vs-in-prompt SOL-guidance comparisons of Section 6.1.1 (Figure 5), producing the labels used to describe curve dominance (e.g., positive signed area indicates the orchestrated Fast-p curve lies higher).
Scalar summaries: geomean and median speedup.

Code has been implemented that computes the geometric mean of per-problem best speedups over PyTorch across the 59-problem evaluation subset, aggregating only integrity-accepted (No or Minor Issues) attempts.

Code has been implemented that computes the median of per-problem best speedups over PyTorch and reports it alongside geomean for each variant (as used in Section 6.1 for GPT-5-mini µCUTLASS+SOL median 1.51× and GPT-5.2 µCUTLASS+SOL median 3.39×).
Speedup retention metric for scheduling analysis.

Code has been implemented that computes speedup retention as the ratio of the geomean (or median) speedup under a scheduling policy to the geomean (or median) speedup under fixed full-budget allocation, expressed as a fraction/percentage.
The retention computation supports both the geomean-retention and median-retention variants used in Figures 7 and 9, and can be evaluated per (ε, w) scheduling policy over replayed run logs.
Efficiency gain metric for SOL-guided budget scheduling.

Code has been implemented that computes efficiency gain = (g_scheduled / τ_scheduled) / (g_fixed / τ_fixed), where g denotes geomean speedup and τ denotes total token cost, so that a value > 1× indicates per-token speedup improvement over fixed allocation.

The efficiency-gain reporting picks, for each variant, the (ε, w) combination that maximizes efficiency gain subject to a ≥95% geomean-retention constraint (as done for Figure 9), and returns the corresponding token-savings and speedup-retention numbers.

Token cost τ used by the efficiency-gain metric is computed by multiplying per-variant total token counts by the model-specific input-token prices ($0.25/M for GPT-5-mini, $1.25/M for GPT-5, $1.75/M for GPT-5.2), matching the normalization used in Section 6.2.

Offline replay infrastructure that runs the integrity pipeline (SOL-ceiling detector, LGD, and PyTorch-only detector) over every attempt in every completed run log, producing per-attempt labels and per-variant aggregate reports.

Code has been implemented that walks each variant's run logs (all four main variants × three model tiers plus MANTIS ablations) and enumerates every attempt with its measured runtime, generated kernel source, NCU profile log, and problem ID for downstream integrity checking.

Code has been implemented that invokes the SOL-ceiling detector, the LGD (with three-way No/Minor/Gaming labeling plus Original vs Inherited Gaming subdivision), and the PyTorch-only detector on each enumerated attempt and stores the resulting labels alongside the attempt metadata.

Code has been implemented that enforces mutual exclusivity of categories: when an attempt is flagged by both the LGD (as Gaming) and the PyTorch-only detector, it is classified as PyTorch-only so that the category counts remain non-overlapping.

Code has been implemented that produces two per-variant speedup rollups: (a) 'pre-filter' geomean/median including all attempts, and (b) 'post-filter' geomean/median excluding attempts labeled Original Gaming, Inherited Gaming, PyTorch-only, or SOL-ceiling-flagged (accepting only No/Minor Issues attempts).
Reproduction of the pre- vs post-filter geomean speedup inflation across all evaluated variants and model tiers, quantifying the reported overstatement without integrity filtering.

Code has been implemented that computes, for each variant × model tier, the ratio of the pre-filter geomean speedup to the post-filter geomean speedup so that inflation factors can be tabulated and compared to the reported ceiling.

The maximum pre-filter-to-post-filter geomean speedup inflation across all evaluated variants and model tiers is up to 1.9× (matching the paper's headline claim that without integrity filtering, reported speedups would inflate by up to 1.9×).
Per-variant inflation ratios are broken out and reported so that the specific variant(s) driving the 1.9× maximum are identified rather than only the aggregate maximum being reported.
Application and reporting of the SOL-ceiling detector across all attempts, using the FP16-based SOL bound and the 10% below-SOL noise buffer.

Code has been implemented that, for each attempt, computes measured_runtime / t_SOL_fp16 and flags the attempt as SOL-ceiling-suspect when measured_runtime < 0.9 × t_SOL_fp16 (i.e., more than 10% below the FP16 SOL bound).
Per-variant counts of SOL-ceiling-flagged attempts are produced and reported (aggregate flag counts and per-model-tier breakdowns), matching the SOL-ceiling flag numbers reported for RQ5.
Code has been implemented that uses the FP16 (not FP32/TF32) SOL bound for the ceiling check so kernels legitimately using FP16/BF16 arithmetic are not falsely flagged, as specified in Section 4.4.

Application of the LLM-based game detector (LGD) with three-way labels (No/Minor Issues/Gaming) and Original vs Inherited Gaming subdivision, and reproduction of the label distributions reported for RQ5.

The LGD prompt supplies the reviewer with the candidate code, the reference PyTorch program, the performance context (measured runtime, PyTorch baseline), and the SOL report, and constrains its output to one of {No Issues, Minor Issues, Gaming} for each attempt.

Code has been implemented that post-processes LGD outputs to split Gaming labels into Original Gaming (a new exploit) and Inherited Gaming (exploit carried over from an earlier attempt on the same problem), by comparing attempt ordering and reused exploit signatures within a problem's trajectory.

The reproduced LGD label distribution across all attempts and variants matches the reported distribution over the four categories (No Issues, Minor Issues, Original Gaming, Inherited Gaming), reproducing the fractional shares reported for RQ5.

Per-variant and per-model-tier LGD label distributions are reported so that variants prone to gaming (e.g., weaker-model or non-µCUTLASS variants) are identified rather than only the aggregate distribution being reported.

The reproduced count of Original Gaming vs Inherited Gaming attempts matches the paper's reported split, demonstrating that once an agent games the system, subsequent attempts inherit the same exploit (as observed in Section 5.8).
Application of the static PyTorch-only detector that parses NCU profile logs and reproduction of the PyTorch-only detection counts reported for RQ5.

Code has been implemented that parses each attempt's NCU profile log, extracts every launched kernel's symbol/signature, and matches it against a library-prefix pattern set including `at::native::`, `cublas`, and `cudnn`.
An attempt is flagged as PyTorch-only iff every profiled kernel matches a library pattern and none are user-written (no agent-authored CUDA/CUTLASS/µCUTLASS kernel appears in the profile).
The reproduced per-variant PyTorch-only flag counts match the paper's reported PyTorch-only detection results for RQ5 (aggregate and per-model-tier).

Reproduction of the KernelBench Level 2 Problem 80 (Gemm_MaxSubtract_GELU) gaming case study, showing that the algebraic collapse to a zero-writing kernel passes the correctness harness while skipping the GEMM.

Code has been implemented that instantiates the L2 Problem 80 reference forward pass (gemm → max over dim=1 with keepdim=True → subtract mean over dim=1 with keepdim=True → GELU) exactly as specified in Section 4.4.

A trivial 'zero-writing' candidate kernel has been implemented that simply outputs an all-zero tensor of the correct shape without performing the GEMM, and it passes the reference correctness check for L2 Problem 80 (demonstrating the algebraic shortcut).

The zero-writing kernel's measured runtime on L2 Problem 80 falls more than 10% below the FP16 SOL bound and is flagged by the SOL-ceiling detector, and is independently labeled Gaming by the LGD when reviewed against the reference and SOL report.

Code has been implemented that records how frequently LLMs exploited the L2 Problem 80 loophole across historical runs, matching the paper's observation that this loophole was exploited frequently enough to warrant excluding the problem from the 59-problem evaluation subset.
Handling of edge cases in the integrity pipeline (accept/reject policy and reporting granularity) that must match the paper's reported RQ5 methodology so downstream speedup numbers reproduce.

Code has been implemented that accepts attempts labeled No Issues or Minor Issues (rather than rejecting Minor Issues), matching the paper's justification that offline review deprives the agent of the chance to fix minor issues in a later attempt.

Code has been implemented that emits a per-variant breakdown table with columns for total attempts, No Issues, Minor Issues, Original Gaming, Inherited Gaming, PyTorch-only, and SOL-ceiling-flagged, enabling side-by-side comparison against the paper's RQ5 tables.

The number of problems whose fastest-per-variant kernel gets removed by integrity filtering is reported per variant, exposing how many top-of-leaderboard results were gamed and had to be replaced by the next-fastest accepted kernel.

Cross-check that the FP16 SOL bound used for RQ5 integrity checking matches the SOLAR-cross-checked FP16 estimates referenced in Section 5.8, so that ceiling flags are computed against the same reference bounds the paper uses.

Code has been implemented that loads the per-problem FP16 SOL estimates cross-checked with SOLAR (with FP32 I/O, perfect fusion, and single-transfer assumptions) and uses them as t_SOL_fp16 for both the SOL-ceiling detector and the scheduling stopping rule, rather than reusing the FP32/TF32 steering estimate.
