sub_tasks.requirements: The comparison against the Sakana AI CUDA Engineer archive (~30K kernels from Claude 3.5 Sonnet on KernelBench H100) is reproduced: for each of the 59 evaluation problems, the fastest correct kernel is picked, the LGD+PyTorch-only detector is run, and the accept/reject-and-fall-through procedure yields the reported per-problem accepted speedups.
The Sakana AI CUDA Engineer Archive is ingested from its published source and prepared per-problem for the 59-problem evaluation subset.

Code has been implemented to fetch the Sakana AI CUDA Engineer archive from the HuggingFace dataset `SakanaAI/AI-CUDA-Engineer-Archive` (accessed circa March 10, 2026) and cache it locally for downstream processing.

Code has been implemented to parse the Sakana AI archive records into (problem_id, kernel_source, correctness_flag, sakana_reported_speedup) tuples across KernelBench Levels 1–3, covering approximately 30,000 kernels generated by Claude 3.5 Sonnet.

Code has been implemented to filter the parsed Sakana AI kernels down to exactly the 59 problem IDs used in the paper's evaluation subset (spanning Levels 1–3), matching the KernelBench (level, problem_id) tuples defined for the study.

Code has been implemented to note the evaluation-environment differences (Sakana AI used PyTorch 2.5.1 / CUDA 12.4 / cuDNN 8.9.7 with wall-clock CUDA-event timing averaged over 2000 runs, versus this paper's NGC PyTorch 2.10.0a0 / CUDA 13.0 with NCU-profiled kernel time) and to use Sakana AI's reported speedups over their own PyTorch baseline directly, without re-running the kernels.
Per-problem candidate ranking selects the fastest correct Sakana AI kernel and produces a descending fall-through list of remaining correct candidates.

Code has been implemented to restrict, on a per-problem basis, the candidate set to Sakana AI kernels marked correct by the archive's own correctness flag, discarding entries labeled incorrect or with missing correctness data.

Code has been implemented to sort each problem's correct-kernel list in descending order of Sakana AI's reported speedup over their PyTorch baseline, so that the head of the list is the fastest correct kernel and subsequent entries form the fall-through queue.

The candidate-selection function, given a problem ID, returns the fastest correct kernel first and, when invoked repeatedly after a rejection, yields the next-fastest correct kernel until the queue is exhausted (at which point the problem is marked as having no accepted kernel).
The LGD (LLM-based Game Detector) plus PyTorch-only detector is applied to each candidate Sakana AI kernel, matching Section 5.8's four-label taxonomy folded for the Sakana comparison.

Code has been implemented to construct the LGD prompt for each Sakana AI candidate that includes (a) the KernelBench reference program, (b) the candidate CUDA/CUTLASS source, (c) performance context including Sakana's reported speedup, and (d) the SOL report for the problem.

Code has been implemented so the LGD returns exactly one label per candidate from the closed set {No Issue, Minor Issue, Gaming, PyTorch-only}, with the PyTorch-only case folded into the LGD (since kernels are not run) rather than requiring a separate NCU-profile pass.

Code has been implemented so the LGD, given a kernel that composes only PyTorch library calls with no agent-written custom CUDA/CUTLASS/µCUTLASS code, deterministically produces the `PyTorch-only` label rather than `No Issue`.

Code has been implemented so that when the LGD flags a kernel with a runtime that would fall more than 10% below the FP16 SOL bound (or that skips the intended computation via an algebraic shortcut), the label is `Gaming` rather than `No Issue` or `Minor Issue`.

Code has been implemented to persist per-candidate LGD outputs (problem_id, kernel identifier, label, rationale) so downstream accept/reject-and-fall-through logic and reporting can consume them without re-invoking the LLM.
The accept/reject-and-fall-through procedure walks each problem's ranked candidate list and returns a single accepted kernel (or none) per problem, as described in Section 5.9.

Code has been implemented so that a candidate labeled `No Issue` or `Minor Issue` is immediately accepted and its Sakana-reported speedup is recorded as the accepted per-problem speedup, with no further candidates evaluated for that problem.

Code has been implemented so that a candidate labeled `Gaming` or `PyTorch-only` is rejected and the procedure advances to the next-fastest correct kernel in the queue rather than terminating for that problem.

Code has been implemented so that when all correct candidates for a problem are exhausted without acceptance, the problem is recorded with no accepted Sakana kernel (rather than defaulting to 1.0× or the fastest-rejected speedup), and is treated consistently by downstream aggregation.

Code has been implemented so that the labels `Gaming` and `PyTorch-only` are mutually exclusive during accept/reject bookkeeping — a kernel flagged as both is counted only as `PyTorch-only`, matching the classification rule in Section 5.8.

Code has been implemented to emit, per problem in the 59-problem subset, a record containing (problem_id, accepted_kernel_id or None, accepted_speedup, number_of_candidates_rejected_before_acceptance, per_candidate_labels) so the Sakana comparison is fully reproducible from logs.

The aggregate comparison between the paper's variants and the integrity-filtered Sakana AI archive is computed and reported, including the specific numerical claims made in the paper's Sakana comparison.

Code has been implemented to compute geomean and median speedup over PyTorch across the 59 problems for the integrity-filtered Sakana AI archive, using the same aggregation convention (per-problem accepted speedup, problems with no accepted kernel handled consistently) used for the paper's own variants.
Code has been implemented to produce a Fast-p curve for the integrity-filtered Sakana AI archive on the 59-problem subset, so it can be overlaid against the paper's variants on the same axes.
The measured geomean speedup over PyTorch of the integrity-filtered Sakana AI archive on the 59-problem subset (Claim 74) matches the paper's reported value within tolerance.

The measured fraction (or count) of the 59 problems for which the integrity-filtered Sakana AI archive yields an accepted kernel with speedup ≥ 1× over PyTorch (Claim 75) matches the paper's reported value within tolerance.

The measured fraction (or count) of the 59 problems for which the integrity-filtered Sakana AI archive yields an accepted kernel with speedup ≥ 2× over PyTorch (Claim 76) matches the paper's reported value within tolerance.

The measured number (or fraction) of the 59 problems whose Sakana AI top-ranked candidate is rejected by the LGD+PyTorch-only detector (labeled Gaming or PyTorch-only) before an accepted kernel is found (Claim 77) matches the paper's reported value within tolerance.

The measured gap between the paper's best variant (e.g., GPT-5.2 µCUTLASS+SOL-guided) geomean speedup and the integrity-filtered Sakana AI archive's geomean speedup on the 59-problem subset (Claim 78) matches the paper's reported value within tolerance.
